raw_response:
# C26 — baseline B candidate answer

The useful approaches found through opened awesome catalogues are preprocessing, conversion to a shared syntax subset, downlevel compilation, and compatibility helpers. The applications to Swift below are my translations of those mechanisms, not claims that the tools implement Swift support or were deployed for this problem.

1. **PreForM — conditional source preprocessing.** https://github.com/szaghi/PreForM
   A package build could set version symbols and use conditional preprocessing to remove incompatible syntax before compilation, while keeping alternatives in one authored tree. Its primary README documents generic-language use and conditional directives. Swift integration and dependable version detection would need to be added. **Date: unknown**; the live README does not establish availability by 2016-01-21.
   Discovery: https://github.com/rabbiabram/awesome-fortran

2. **Python-Future — shared-source compatibility and conversion.** https://python-future.org/index.html
   Its compatibility layer and futurize/pasteurize workflow suggest normalizing source into forms that work across versions, with helpers for differences that remain. The syntax guide gives shared forms for print and exceptions. This is a Python implementation; Swift would need its own rewrite rules and semantic checks. **Date: pre-decision for the historical mechanism**: the opened changelog includes a syntax-related helper in 0.13.0 (2014-08-13) and a forward-compatible exec conversion in 0.15.1 (2015-09-09). Current guide details are not backdated.
   Verification: https://python-future.org/changelog.html and https://python-future.org/compatible_idioms.html
   Discovery: https://github.com/DarLiner/awesome-python

3. **Babel — downlevel source compilation.** https://github.com/babel/babel
   Compiling newer features into syntax understood by older targets is an alternative way to keep one authored source tree. It requires build tooling and language-specific transformations; generated outputs may differ by target. **Date: unknown**; only live evidence was opened, including a later JavaScript syntax example, so no pre-cutoff availability is claimed here.
   Discovery: https://github.com/milahu/awesome-transpilers

4. **Python-Modernize — conversion to a shared syntax subset.** https://github.com/mitsuhiko/python-modernize
   Automated fixers could help maintainers rewrite version-specific constructs into a common grammar and compatibility calls. Its documentation describes attempted Python 2.6+/3 compatibility and explicitly does not guarantee the output; the normal workflow depends on six. This is an author-time tooling analogue requiring Swift-specific work. **Date: unknown**; the opened changelog has version numbers without dates.
   Verification: https://github.com/mitsuhiko/python-modernize/blob/master/CHANGELOG.rst
   Discovery: https://github.com/DarLiner/awesome-python

5. **Six 1.10.0 — a distributable compatibility module.** https://pypi.org/project/six/1.10.0/
   Centralized helper calls can absorb version differences without duplicating an entire source tree, and a one-file module is convenient for source distribution. This only handles differences expressible in grammar both versions accept; an older parser still needs preprocessing or rewriting for unknown syntax. **Date: pre-decision**; the opened version-specific package and source-archive record is dated 2015-10-07.
   Discovery: https://github.com/DarLiner/awesome-python

The main design distinction is when the incompatibility is handled: preprocessing can remove text before parsing, transformation can generate acceptable grammar, and compatibility helpers require an already parseable common form. No tool was installed or tested against Swift.

This was an internal-model translation exercise, not a human or different-model comparison. Discovery used three catalogue-targeted searches and four opened awesome lists. Verification made 18 explicit open/click attempts, with five additional find inspections of already opened pages; the conservative retrieval total is 23 of 25. One excluded rust-lang/rfcs search snippet was seen and not opened. All accepted candidates have an opened catalogue and opened primary evidence.

budget.counting_method: opened_pages conservatively includes all 18 explicit open/click attempts, including reopens, plus five find inspections; searches are counted separately.

limitations: Only the rules and assigned prefix were read for local task content; no gold, other prefixes or runs, judgments, target proposal, or repository history were read.

Catalogue targeting used awesome-list search terms on GitHub; search results also included non-catalogue false positives. These were not used for candidate discovery or opened. The exact queries and excluded snippet exposure are retained.
All primary verification followed opened catalogue links; later primary pages were inspected only to verify already discovered candidates.
All four catalogue pages are live, with unknown historical catalogue availability; their present listings are not asserted to have existed before the cutoff.
Pre-decision labels for Python-Future and Six rely on opened dated historical entries or a version-specific release; undated live evidence for PreForM, Babel and Python-Modernize remains unknown.
The latest Six package page is post-decision evidence and is marked accordingly; the accepted Six candidate is the separately opened 1.10.0 release.

Find inspections were performed on already opened pages: gribouille/awesome-python twice, awesome-fortran once, Babel once and PreForM once. The PreForM find for conditional returned no match, after which a targeted reopen supplied its feature list. Individual find timestamps were not separately sampled; their URLs and order are preserved through the page records and this note.
No blocked or failed URL opening was returned. An opened page sometimes initially supplied only its title, and these were reopened or inspected before relying on their contents.
These are mechanism-transfer candidates, not ready-made Swift solutions, and no installation, compilation, deployment or usefulness test was performed.
Model pretraining knowledge cannot be erased; memory leakage is not controlled. No target proposal identity was deliberately inferred or retrieved.
Translation was performed by GPT-6 Astra Pro in an internal separate context, not by a human or a different model.
